A staff-role user can point this at internal services or cloud metadata endpoints (e.g. http://169.254.169.254/...) and the fetched content is stored as a document version, making it retrievable afterward. Contrast with clients.$id.tsx's syncClientLogoFromUrl, which validates the hostname against an explicit allowlist before fetching — that check is missing here.

packageExportBundle(csvContent, reportType) builds a shell command string by directly interpolating `reportType` and runs it with `spawn(cmd, [], { shell: true })` (line 65: `spawn(\`tar czf ${archivePath} -C ${workDir} export.csv --transform s|export.csv|${reportType}.csv|\`, [], { shell: true })`). `reportType` comes from the unsanitized form field `reportType` submitted via the 'exportMattersBundle' intent (action(), line 256: `const reportType = ((formData.get("reportType") as string) || "matters").trim();`), so a firm_admin-role attacker can inject shell metacharacters (e.g. `; rm -rf / #` or `$(...)`) to execute arbitrary OS commands on the server. The sibling function packageRetentionExportBundle validates reportType against an allowlist and uses `spawn("tar", [...], { shell: false })`, showing the safe pattern that this path fails to follow.

renderPrintLetterhead(layout, document) calls `Handlebars.compile(layout)` where `layout` is the raw, attacker-controlled `layout` query-string parameter (loader(), line 52: `const customLayout = url.searchParams.get("layout")`, compiled at line 53-61). Handlebars templates support helpers and, depending on version/registered helpers, can be abused for server-side template injection leading to code execution or, at minimum, arbitrary HTML injection. The compiled output is then rendered client-side via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: letterhead }}` (component, line 72), so even absent full SSTI this is a straightforward stored/reflected XSS vector — any authenticated user who can view a document can trigger arbitrary HTML/script execution in another viewer's browser by sharing a crafted `?layout=` URL.

applyPreferencesPayload(userId, rawJson) parses a client-supplied JSON blob and passes the result directly as the `data` object to `db.user.update({ where: { id: userId }, data: preferences })` with no field allowlist. The 'updatePreferences' intent (action(), lines 55-63) reaches this with `preferencesJson` taken verbatim from the POST body. Although the UI only ever sends `{name: user.name}` (line 243), an attacker can submit `preferencesJson` containing arbitrary User model fields such as `role`, `isActive`, `email`, or `passwordHash` for their own account (self-service update, `where: { id: userId }` uses the caller's own id), enabling full privilege escalation to firm_admin. Compare to workspace.server.ts's applyWidgetPreferenceEdits, which allowlists specific keys before merging — that pattern is missing here for a live Prisma model update.

extra.message: searchStaffByEmail(searchTerm) builds the LDAP filter `(mail=${searchTerm})` by direct string interpolation with no escaping of LDAP special characters, then passes it to `client.search(BASE_DN, { filter }, ...)`. The value flows from user input: clients.new.tsx's runDirectoryConflictCheck (line 79) takes the raw `directoryTerm` form field from the 'checkDirectoryConflict' intent (line 130: `const directoryTerm = ((formData.get("directoryTerm") as string) || "").trim();`) and passes it straight through to searchStaffByEmail (line 85), letting an authenticated paralegal/attorney inject LDAP filter metacharacters (e.g. `*)(uid=*))(|(mail=*`) to alter query logic and enumerate or bypass directory search restrictions. The sibling function verifyGroupAccess in the same file correctly escapes both interpolated values via escapeLdapFilterValue() (line 42) — that sanitization is missing here.

The loader checks access with `canAccessDocument(user.id, id)` against the `id` route param (line 16), but when a `versionId` query parameter is supplied it fetches that version directly by its own id (`db.documentVersion.findUnique({ where: { id: versionId }, ... })`, lines 27-32) without verifying `version.documentId === id` or re-checking access against the version's actual parent document. A user who has legitimate access to any one document can enumerate `versionId` values belonging to other documents/matters (including privileged or highly-confidential ones they cannot otherwise access) and download their file content, bypassing the authorization check entirely.

extra.message: resolveDocumentViewScope(request, documentId, userId) reads the raw `viewAccess` cookie directly off the request (`request.headers.get("Cookie")`, unsigned, not part of the app's signed session) and, if its value is the literal string `"firm-wide"`, returns `true` unconditionally — completely bypassing the real `canAccessDocument` authorization check. extra.message: The action() handler takes the `x-return-url` request header verbatim and redirects to it with no validation of scheme or origin: `const returnTo = request.headers.get("x-return-url"); if (returnTo) { throw redirect(returnTo); }`. Any value supplied in that header — including a fully-qualified external URL — is honored, allowing an attacker to craft a request that redirects an authenticated co-counsel session to an arbitrary phishing destination. Contrast with messages.tsx's resolveTrustedReturnDestination, which parses the destination and rejects any URL whose origin doesn't match `process.env.APP_ORIGIN` before redirecting — that allowlist check is absent here.

extra.message: saveUploadedFile builds the on-disk filename as `${uuidv4()}-${file.name}` (line 49) and writes it with `path.join(dir, uniqueName)` (line 50) without stripping path separators or `..` sequences from `file.name`. `file.name` comes from the multipart upload's client-supplied filename field, which is fully attacker-controllable independent of any `<input type=file>` client-side restriction (e.g. via a raw multipart POST). A crafted filename such as `../../../../etc/cron.d/evil` (or an absolute path) can cause `path.join` to resolve outside the intended matter upload directory, allowing a staff-role user to write files to arbitrary locations on the server (invoked from matters.$id.tsx's 'uploadDocument' intent, line 235, and documents.$id.tsx's 'uploadNewVersion' intent, line 169).

persistMatterViewSnapshot(viewLabel, payload) and readMatterViewSnapshot(viewLabel) build a file path as `path.join(dir, \`${viewLabel}.json\`)` with no sanitization of `viewLabel` (contrast with the neighboring persistTaskDraftNote, which explicitly applies `path.basename(noteLabel)` first). `viewLabel` originates from the client-controlled `matterViewLabel` cookie read in matters.$id.tsx's 'saveViewLayout' action handler (lines 161-165: `const cookieMatch = cookieHeader.match(/matterViewLabel=([^;]+)/); const viewLabel = cookieMatch ? decodeURIComponent(cookieMatch[1]) : "default"; persistMatterViewSnapshot(viewLabel, layoutJson);`). An attacker who controls this cookie value can supply a traversal sequence (e.g. `../../../../tmp/evil`) to write or read arbitrary JSON files outside the intended `data/view-cache` directory.

createCoCounselAccessToken issues the `collab_ctx` cookie as `\`collab_ctx=${encodeURIComponent(token)}; Path=/; Max-Age=${60 * 60 * 24 * 365}\`` with no `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, or `SameSite` attributes, and the token is valid for a full year with no expiry check in validateCoCounselAccessToken. This cookie carries a bearer-style credential granting external co-counsel access to a matter; without `HttpOnly` it is readable by any script (XSS anywhere on the origin can exfiltrate it), and without `Secure`/`SameSite` it can be sent over plaintext HTTP or leaked via cross-site requests. Contrast with createClientPortalFeedToken in the same file, which sets `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` on its equivalent cookie — that hardening is missing here.

extra.message: buildComplianceReport(request) reveals the raw exception message and stack trace whenever the request carries an `x-app-context` header (`const appContext = request.headers.get("x-app-context"); if (appContext) { return { ok: false as const, error: err?.message, stack: err?.stack }; }`), rather than gating verbose diagnostics on a trusted server-side signal (e.g. NODE_ENV, as buildBillingSummary in admin.export.tsx correctly does).
